modern: In *the evening of the day* opportunities are plentiful. People come home from work, and the eager soul-winner finds time to spread the news of Jesus’ love. Have I no evening work for Jesus? If not, let me no longer hold back my hand from a service that needs plenty of labor. Sinners are perishing for lack of knowledge; whoever loiters may find the hem of his clothes crimson with the blood of souls. Jesus gave both his hands to the nails; how can I keep back one of mine from his blessed work? Night and day he toiled and prayed for me; how can I give a single hour to pampering my flesh with luxurious ease? Up, idle heart; stretch out your hand to work, or lift it up to pray. Heaven and hell are in earnest; let me be in earnest too, and sow good seed this evening for the Lord my God.

*The evening of life* has its calls too. Life is so short that a morning of manhood’s strength and an evening of decline make up the whole of it. To some it seems long, but then fourpence is a great sum of money to a poor man. Life is so brief that no one can afford to lose a day. It has been well said that if a great king brought us a great heap of gold and told us to take as much as we could count in a day, we would make a long day of it. We would start early in the morning, and in the evening we wouldn’t hold back our hand. But winning souls is far nobler work; how is it that we pull back from it so soon?

Some are spared to a long evening of green old age. If that is my case, let me use whatever gifts I still have, and serve my blessed and faithful Lord to the last hour. By his grace I will die in harness, and lay down my charge only when I lay down my body. Age may teach the young, cheer the faint and encourage the downhearted. If evening has less of youthful heat, it should have more of calm wisdom; so in the evening I won’t hold back my hand.

modern:
How heartening to the believer is the delight God takes in his saints! We can’t see any reason in ourselves why the Lord should take pleasure in us. We can’t take delight in ourselves, for we often have to groan under our burdens, aware of our sinfulness and grieving over our unfaithfulness. And we fear that God’s people can’t take much delight in us either, for they must see so much of our imperfections and follies that they may sooner grieve over our weaknesses than admire our graces. But we love to dwell on this surpassing truth, this glorious mystery: that as the bridegroom rejoices over the bride, so the Lord rejoices over us.

We don’t read anywhere that God delights in the cloud-capped mountains or the sparkling stars, but we do read that he delights in the inhabited parts of the earth, and that his delights are with the sons of men. We don’t find it written that even angels delight his soul; nor does he say of cherubim and seraphim, “Thou shalt be called Hephzibah, for the Lord delighteth in thee.” But he does say all that to poor fallen creatures like us, debased and corrupted by sin, but saved, lifted up and glorified by his grace.

In what strong language he expresses his delight in his people! Who could have imagined the eternal One bursting into song? Yet it is written, “He will rejoice over thee with joy, he will rest in his love, he will joy over thee with singing.” As he looked at the world he had made, he said, “It is very good”; but when he saw those who are the purchase of Jesus’ blood, his own chosen ones, it seemed as if the great heart of the Infinite could hold back no longer, but overflowed in divine shouts of joy. Shouldn’t we give our grateful answer to such a marvelous declaration of his love, and sing, “I will rejoice in the Lord, I will joy in the God of my salvation?”

modern:
Fear made David pray like this, for something whispered, “Perhaps, after all, you may be gathered with the wicked.” That fear, though spoiled by unbelief, springs mainly from a holy anxiety that comes from remembering past sin. Even the pardoned man will ask, “What if at the end my sins should be remembered, and I should be left out of the catalogue of the saved?” He remembers how unfruitful he is now—so little grace, so little love, so little holiness. Looking ahead, he considers his weakness and the many temptations that surround him, and he fears he may fall and become the enemy’s prey. A sense of sin and present evil, and of the corruptions that so often win, makes him pray in fear and trembling, “Gather not my soul with sinners.”

Reader, if you have prayed this prayer, and if your character fits the description in the psalm it comes from, you needn’t be afraid of being gathered with sinners. Do you have the two virtues David had: outwardly walking in integrity, and inwardly trusting in the Lord? Are you resting on Christ’s sacrifice, and can you go around God’s altar with humble hope? If so, be sure of this: you will never be gathered with the wicked, for that disaster is impossible. The gathering at the judgment is like to like. “Gather ye together first the tares, and bind them in bundles to burn them: but gather the wheat into my barn.” If, then, you are *like* God’s people, you will be *with* God’s people.

You can’t be gathered with the wicked, for you were bought at too high a price. Redeemed by the blood of Christ, you are his forever, and where he is, his people must be. You are loved too much to be thrown away with the rejected. Will someone dear to Christ perish? Impossible! Hell can’t hold you! Heaven claims you! Trust in your Surety and don’t be afraid!

notes.note: “…nor my life with bloody men” ([[Ps.26.9|Psalm 26:9]]).

modern:
Be glad at heart, believer, but make sure your gladness has its source *in the Lord*. You have plenty of reason to be glad in your God, for you can sing with David, “God, my exceeding joy.” Be glad that the Lord reigns, that Jehovah is King! Rejoice that he sits on the throne and rules all things! Every attribute of God should become a fresh ray in the sunlight of our gladness. That he is wise should make us glad, knowing as we do how foolish we are. That he is *mighty* should make us rejoice, since we tremble at our own weakness. That he is everlasting should always be a theme of joy, when we know that we wither like the grass. That he is *unchanging* should give us a song without end, since *we* change every hour. That he is full of grace, overflowing with it, and that he has given this grace to us in covenant; that it is ours to cleanse us, ours to keep us, ours to sanctify us, ours to perfect us, ours to bring us to glory—all this should make us glad in him.

This gladness in God is like a deep river. So far we have only touched its edge; we know a little of its clear, sweet, heavenly streams, but farther out the water is deeper and the current rushes on with more joy. The Christian feels that he may delight not only in what God is, but also in everything God *has done* in the past. The Psalms show us that God’s people in the old days used to think a great deal about God’s actions, and to have a song for each of them. So let God’s people today tell over the deeds of the Lord! Let them tell of his mighty acts, and “sing unto the Lord, for he hath triumphed gloriously.” And let them never stop singing; for as new mercies flow to them day by day, so their gladness in the Lord’s loving acts, in providence and in grace, should show itself in unending thanksgiving. Be glad, you children of Zion, and rejoice in the Lord your God.

modern:
Most of us know what it is to be overwhelmed in heart: emptied, the way a man wipes a dish and turns it upside down; swamped and knocked over on our side like a ship overpowered by the storm. Discovering the corruption within us will do this, if the Lord lets the great deep of our depravity be stirred up and throw up mud and dirt. Disappointments and heartbreaks will do it, when wave after wave rolls over us and we are like a broken shell flung back and forth by the surf. Thank God, at such times we aren’t left without a comfort that is all we need. Our God is the harbor for weather-beaten sails, the shelter for lonely, worn-out pilgrims. He is higher than we are: his mercy higher than our sins, his love higher than our thoughts. It’s pitiful to see people putting their trust in something lower than themselves; but our confidence is fixed on a Lord who is exceedingly high and glorious. He is a Rock because he doesn’t change, and a high Rock because the storms that overwhelm us roll far below at his feet. They don’t disturb him; he rules them as he pleases. If we get under the shelter of this lofty Rock, we can defy the hurricane; all is calm on the sheltered side of that towering cliff.

But sadly, the troubled mind is often thrown into such confusion that we need to be piloted to this divine shelter. That’s why the text is a prayer. O Lord, our God, by your Holy Spirit, teach us the way of faith; lead us into your rest. The wind is blowing us out to sea; the helm won’t answer to our feeble hand. You, and you alone, can steer us over the bar between those sunken rocks, safely into the fair haven. How dependent we are on you: we need you to bring us to you. To be wisely guided and steered into safety and peace is your gift, and yours alone. Tonight, be pleased to deal kindly with your servants.

notes.note: “From the end of the earth will I cry unto thee, when my heart is overwhelmed: lead me to the rock that is higher than I” ([[Ps.61.2|Psalm 61:2]]).

modern:
What a privileged position! It includes our *justification* before God, but the word for “acceptance” in the Greek means more than that. It means that we are objects of *divine pleasure*, no, even of *divine delight*. How marvelous that we—worms, mortals, sinners—should be the objects of divine love! But it is only “*in the beloved*.”

Some Christians seem to think they are accepted on the strength of their own experience; at least, that is how they understand it. When their spirits are lively and their hopes are bright, they think God accepts them, because they feel so high, so heavenly-minded, so lifted above the earth! But when their souls cling to the dust, they fall victim to the fear that they are no longer accepted. If only they could see that all their high joys don’t raise them, and all their low moods don’t really lower them, in their Father’s sight! They stand accepted in One who never changes, in One who is always the beloved of God, always perfect, always without spot or wrinkle or any such thing. How much happier they would be, and how much more they would honor the Savior!

So rejoice in this, believer: you are accepted “in the beloved.” You look within and say, “There is nothing acceptable *here*!” But look at Christ, and see whether there isn’t everything acceptable *there*. Your sins trouble you; but God has thrown your sins behind his back, and you are accepted in the Righteous One. You have to fight corruption and wrestle with temptation, but you are already accepted in him who has overcome the powers of evil. The devil tempts you; cheer up, he can’t destroy you, for you are accepted in him who has crushed Satan’s head. Know your glorious standing with full assurance. Even the souls in glory are not more accepted than you are. They are accepted in heaven only “in the beloved,” and even now you are accepted in Christ in exactly the same way.

modern:
A man had a son possessed by a demon, a spirit that made him unable to speak. The father had seen the disciples try to heal his child and fail, and so he had little or no faith in Christ. When he was told to bring his son to him, he said to Jesus, “If thou canst do anything, have compassion on us, and help us.” Now there was an “if” in the question, but the poor trembling father had put the “if” in the wrong place. So Jesus, without telling him to take the “if” back, kindly moved it to its proper place. “No, indeed,” he seemed to say, “there should be no ‘if’ about my power, or about my willingness. The ‘if’ lies somewhere else.” “*If thou canst believe*, all things are possible to him that believeth.” The man’s trust grew stronger; he offered a humble prayer for more faith; and at once Jesus spoke the word, and the demon was driven out, with orders never to return.

There is a lesson here that we need to learn. Like this man, we often see that there is an “if” somewhere, but we keep blundering by putting it in the wrong place. “*If*” Jesus can help me, “*if*” he can give me grace to overcome temptation, “*if*” he can give me pardon, “*if*” he can make me successful? No, “*if*” you can believe, he both can and will. You have misplaced your “if.” If you can trust with confidence, then just as all things are possible to Christ, so all things will be possible to you. Faith stands in God’s power and is robed in God’s majesty. It wears the royal robes and rides the King’s horse, for it is the grace the King delights to honor. Wrapping itself in the glorious might of the Spirit, who works all things, it becomes mighty in the omnipotence of God: mighty to do, to dare and to suffer. All things, without limit, are possible to him who believes. My soul, can you believe your Lord tonight?

modern:
For many reasons an armed escort would have been welcome for the band of pilgrims, but a holy sense of shame would not let Ezra ask for one. He was afraid the pagan king would think his professions of faith in God were mere hypocrisy, or would imagine that the God of Israel couldn’t protect his own worshipers. He couldn’t bring himself to lean on an arm of flesh in a matter so plainly the Lord’s. And so the caravan set out with no visible protection, guarded by him who is the sword and shield of his people.

I’m afraid few believers feel this holy jealousy for God. Even those who walk by faith to some degree sometimes spoil the shine of their lives by begging for help from people. It is a most blessed thing to have no props and no buttresses, but to stand upright on the Rock of Ages, held up by the Lord alone. Would any believers look for state funding for their church if they remembered that the Lord is dishonored when they ask for Caesar’s help? As if the Lord couldn’t supply the needs of his own cause! Would we run so quickly to friends and relatives for help if we remembered that the Lord is magnified when we rely completely on his arm alone? My soul, wait only on God.

“But,” someone says, “aren’t we supposed to use means?” Of course we are; but our fault seldom lies in neglecting them. Far more often it comes from foolishly believing in them instead of believing in God. Few go too far in neglecting human help, but very many sin greatly by making too much of it. Learn, dear reader, to glorify the Lord by leaving means untried, if using them would dishonor the name of the Lord.

modern:
Christian experience is full of paradoxes, and here is one: the bride was asleep, and yet she was awake. Only someone who has plowed with the heifer of his own experience can solve the believer’s riddle. The two points in tonight’s text are a mournful sleepiness and a hopeful wakefulness.

*I sleep.* Through the sin that lives in us we can grow slack in holy duties, lazy in worship, dull in spiritual joys, and altogether sluggish and careless. This is a shameful state for someone in whom the life-giving Spirit lives, and it is dangerous in the highest degree. Even wise virgins sometimes doze, but it is high time for all of us to shake off the chains of laziness. I’m afraid many believers lose their strength as Samson lost his hair, while sleeping in the lap of carnal security. With a perishing world around us, sleeping is cruel; with eternity so close at hand, it is madness. Yet none of us is as awake as we should be. A few claps of thunder would do us all good, and unless we soon rouse ourselves, we may get them, in the form of war, or epidemic, or personal bereavements and losses. Oh, that we may leave the couch of fleshly ease forever, and go out with flaming torches to meet the coming Bridegroom!

*My heart waketh.* This is a happy sign. Life isn’t gone, though it is sadly smothered. When our renewed heart struggles against our natural heaviness, we should be grateful to sovereign grace for keeping a little life within the body of this death. Jesus will hear our hearts, will help our hearts, will visit our hearts; for the voice of the wakeful heart is really the voice of our Beloved, saying, “Open to me.” Holy zeal will surely unbolt the door.

modern:
Being justified by faith, we have peace with God. Conscience no longer accuses. Judgment now rules for the sinner instead of against him. Memory looks back on past sins with deep sorrow for the sin, but with no dread of any penalty to come. For Christ has paid his people’s debt to the last jot and tittle, and received God’s receipt; and unless God could be so unjust as to demand double payment for one debt, no soul for whom Jesus died as a substitute can ever be thrown into hell.

It seems to be one of the very principles of our enlightened nature to believe that God is just. We feel that it must be so, and at first this is what terrifies us. But isn’t it marvelous that this very same belief, that God is just, later becomes the pillar of our confidence and peace? If God is just, I, a sinner, alone and without a substitute, must be punished. But Jesus stands in my place and is punished for me; and now, if God is just, I, a sinner standing in Christ, can never be punished. God would have to change his nature before one soul for whom Jesus was a substitute could ever, by any possibility, suffer the lash of the law. So, since Jesus has taken the believer’s place, and has given divine wrath the full equivalent of all that his people should have suffered for their sin, the believer can shout in glorious triumph, “Who shall lay anything to the charge of God’s elect?” Not God, for he has justified; not Christ, for he has died, “yea rather hath risen again.”

My hope lives, not because I am not a sinner, but because I am a sinner for whom Christ died. My trust is not that I am holy, but that, unholy as I am, *he* is my righteousness. My faith rests not on what I am, or will be, or feel, or know, but on what Christ is, on what he has done, and on what he is doing for me now. On the lion of justice the fair maiden of hope rides like a queen.

modern:
The human mind looks for rest, and by nature it looks for it apart from the Lord Jesus Christ. Educated people are apt, even after they are converted, to look on the simple truths of the cross of Christ with too little reverence and love. They are caught in the same old net that caught the Greeks, and have a hankering to mix philosophy with revelation. The temptation for a person of refined thought and higher education is to drift away from the simple truth of Christ crucified and invent, as they put it, a more *intellectual* doctrine. This is what led the early Christian churches into Gnosticism and bewitched them with all sorts of heresies. This is the root of Neology and the other fine things that were so fashionable in Germany in days gone by, and that now so entangle certain kinds of ministers.

Whoever you are, dear reader, and whatever your education, if you are the Lord’s, you can be sure you will find no rest in philosophizing theology. You may accept this teaching of one great thinker, or that dream of another deep reasoner, but what chaff is to the wheat, they will be to the pure word of God. All that reason can discover, even at its best, is only the ABC of truth, and even that lacks certainty; while in Christ Jesus all the fullness of wisdom and knowledge is stored up. Every attempt by Christians to be content with systems that Unitarian and Broad Church thinkers would approve must fail. True heirs of heaven must come back to the grandly simple reality that makes the plowboy’s eyes flash with joy and gladdens the godly pauper’s heart: “Jesus Christ came into the world to save sinners.” Jesus satisfies the loftiest intellect when he is received in faith, but apart from him the mind of the regenerate finds no rest. “The fear of the Lord is the beginning of knowledge.” “A good understanding have all they that do his commandments.”

modern:
The vision in this chapter describes the condition of Israel in Zechariah’s day; but read as it applies to us, it describes the Church of God as we find it in the world today. The Church is compared to a grove of myrtles flourishing in a valley. It is *hidden*: unnoticed, tucked away, seeking no honor and drawing no attention from the careless passerby. The Church, like her Head, has a glory, but it is hidden from fleshly eyes, for the time when she will break out in all her splendor hasn’t come yet.

The picture also suggests *quiet security*. The myrtle grove in the valley is still and calm while the storm sweeps over the mountaintops. Storms spend their force on the craggy peaks of the Alps, but down below, where the river flows that makes glad the city of our God, the myrtles flourish by the still waters, unshaken by the raging wind. How great is the inner peace of God’s Church! Even when she is opposed and persecuted, she has a peace that the world doesn’t give, and so the world can’t take it away: the peace of God which passes all understanding guards the hearts and minds of God’s people.

Doesn’t the picture vividly show the peaceful, *perpetual growth* of the saints? The myrtle doesn’t shed her leaves; she is always green. And the Church, even in her worst times, still has a blessed freshness of grace about her; in fact, she has sometimes been at her *greenest* when her winter has been sharpest. She has prospered most when her troubles have been most severe. So the text *hints at victory*. The myrtle is the emblem of peace, and a telling sign of *triumph*. The brows of conquerors were crowned with myrtle and with laurel; and isn’t the Church always victorious? Isn’t every Christian more than a conqueror through him who loved him? Living in peace, don’t the saints fall asleep in the arms of victory?

modern: When the crash of a falling oak is heard in the forest, it’s a sign that the woodcutter is out, and every tree in the whole wood may tremble in case the sharp edge of the ax finds it tomorrow. We are all like trees marked for the ax, and the fall of one should remind us that for every one of us, whether great like the cedar or humble like the fir, the appointed hour is creeping on fast. I hope that hearing of death so often doesn’t make us callous to it. May we never be like the birds in the steeple, which build their nests while the bells are tolling, and sleep quietly while the solemn funeral peals are startling the air. May we treat death as the weightiest of all events, and be sobered as it approaches. It isn’t right for us to play while our eternal destiny hangs by a thread. The sword is out of its sheath: let’s not trifle. It is polished, and the edge is sharp: let’s not play with it. Anyone who doesn’t prepare for death is more than an ordinary fool; he is a madman. When the voice of God is heard among the trees of the garden, let fig tree and sycamore, elm and cedar alike, hear its sound.

Be ready, servant of Christ, for your Master is coming suddenly, when an ungodly world least expects him. Make sure you are faithful in his work, for your grave will soon be dug. Be ready, parents: see that your children are brought up in the fear of God, for they must soon be orphans. Be ready, business people: make sure your affairs are in order, and that you serve God with all your hearts, for the days of your service here on earth will soon be over, and you will be called to give account for the deeds done in the body, whether they are good or evil. May we all prepare for the judgment seat of the great King with a care that will be rewarded with his gracious praise, “Well done, good and faithful servant.”

modern:
Anyone who claims that Christianity makes people miserable is a complete stranger to it himself. It would be strange indeed if it made us wretched, for look *what a position it raises us to*! It makes us sons of God. Do you suppose God will give all the happiness to his enemies and keep all the mourning for his own family? Will his enemies have fun and joy, while the children born in his own house inherit sorrow and misery? Will the sinner who has no share in Christ call himself rich in happiness, while we go around mourning as if we were penniless beggars? No, we will rejoice in the Lord always and glory in our inheritance, for we “have not received the spirit of bondage again to fear; but we have received the spirit of adoption, whereby we cry, Abba, Father.” The rod of discipline must fall on us in our measure, but it produces in us the comforting fruits of righteousness; and so, with the help of the divine Comforter, we, the “people saved of the Lord,” will rejoice in the God of our salvation.

We are married to Christ; and will our great Bridegroom let his bride go on in constant grief? Our hearts are bound to him: we are his members, and though for a while we may suffer as our Head once suffered, we are already blessed with heavenly blessings in him. We have the down payment on our inheritance in the comforts of the Spirit, which are neither few nor small. Heirs of joy forever, we have foretastes of our portion. There are streaks of the light of joy to announce our eternal sunrise. Our riches are beyond the sea; our city with firm foundations lies on the other side of the river; gleams of glory from the spirit world cheer our hearts and urge us on. Truly it is said of us, “Happy art thou, O Israel; who is like unto thee, O people saved by the Lord?”

modern:
Knocking wasn’t enough, for my heart was too full of sleep, too cold and ungrateful to get up and open the door; but the touch of his effective grace has stirred my soul. Oh, the patience of my Beloved, to wait there when he found himself shut out, and me asleep on the bed of laziness! Oh, the greatness of his patience, to knock and knock again, and to add his voice to his knocking, pleading with me to open to him! How could I have refused him? Shameful heart, blush and be ashamed! But this is the greatest kindness of all: he becomes his own doorkeeper and unbolts the door himself. Three times blessed is the hand that stoops to lift the latch and turn the key. Now I see that nothing but my Lord’s own power can save such a worthless mass of wickedness as I am. The ordinances fail; even the gospel has no effect on me until his hand is stretched out. Now I also see that his hand succeeds where everything else fails: he can open when nothing else will. Blessed be his name, I feel his gracious presence even now.

Well may my heart be moved for him, when I think of all he has suffered for me, and of how meanly I have repaid him. I have let my affections wander. I have set up rivals. I have grieved him. Sweetest and dearest of all loves, I have treated you the way an unfaithful wife treats her husband. Oh, my cruel sins, my cruel self! What can I do? Tears are a poor show of my repentance; my whole heart boils with anger at myself. Wretch that I am, to treat my Lord, my All in All, my exceeding great joy, as though he were a stranger! Jesus, you forgive freely, but that isn’t enough: keep me from being unfaithful in the future. Kiss away these tears, and then purify my heart and bind it to yourself with sevenfold cords, never to wander again.

modern:
Perhaps no figure of speech shows God in a more gracious light than when he is pictured as stooping from his throne and coming down from heaven to attend to the needs and see the sorrows of humanity. We love him who, when Sodom and Gomorrah were full of wickedness, wouldn’t destroy those cities until he had visited them in person. We can’t help pouring out our hearts in love for our Lord, who bends his ear down from the highest glory and puts it to the lips of the dying sinner whose failing heart longs to be reconciled. How can we help loving him, when we know that he numbers the very hairs of our heads, marks our path and orders our ways?

This great truth comes especially close to our hearts when we remember how attentive he is, not only to his creatures’ earthly interests, but to their spiritual concerns. Though vast distances lie between the finite creature and the infinite Creator, there are links that join them. When you shed a tear, don’t think God doesn’t see it; for “Like as a father pitieth his children, so the Lord pitieth them that fear him.” Your sigh can move the heart of Jehovah; your whisper can bend his ear to you; your prayer can hold back his hand; your faith can move his arm. Don’t think God sits on high taking no notice of you. Remember that however poor and needy you are, the Lord still thinks about you. For the eyes of the Lord run back and forth through the whole earth, to show himself strong on behalf of those whose hearts are perfect toward him.

modern:
Success is certain when the Lord has promised it. You may have pleaded month after month without any sign of an answer, but it isn’t possible for the Lord to be deaf when his people are earnest about something that concerns his glory. The prophet on the top of Carmel kept wrestling with God, and never for a moment gave in to the fear that his case would be thrown out of Jehovah’s court. Six times the servant came back, but each time the only word spoken was “Go again.” We mustn’t dream of unbelief, but hold on to our faith even to seventy times seven. Faith sends hope out, full of expectation, to look from the brow of Carmel; and if nothing is seen, she sends her again and again. Far from being crushed by repeated disappointment, faith is spurred on to plead with her God more earnestly. She is humbled, but not put off. Her groans are deeper and her sighs more intense, but she never loosens her grip or holds back her hand.

Flesh and blood would find a quick answer more pleasant, but believing souls have learned to submit, and to find it good to wait *for* the Lord as well as *upon* him. Delayed answers often set the heart searching itself, and so lead to sorrow for sin and spiritual renewal. In this way deadly blows are struck at our corruption, and the chambers of imagery are cleansed. The great danger is that people lose heart and miss the blessing. Reader, don’t fall into that sin, but keep on praying and watching. At last the little cloud was seen, the sure forerunner of torrents of rain; and so it will be with you. The sign of good will surely be given, and you will rise like a prince who has prevailed, to enjoy the mercy you have sought. Elijah was a man of like passions with us; his power with God didn’t lie in his own merits. If his believing prayer accomplished so much, why not yours? Plead the precious blood with unceasing persistence, and it will be with you as you desire.

modern:
This rule seems strange enough, yet there was wisdom in it: the disease coming out all over the skin proved that the body underneath was sound. This morning it will do us good to see what this unusual rule pictures for us. We, too, are lepers, and may read the law of the leper as applying to ourselves. When someone sees himself to be altogether lost and ruined, covered all over with the defilement of sin, with no part free from pollution; when he disowns all righteousness of his own and pleads guilty before the Lord, then he is clean through the blood of Jesus and the grace of God. Hidden, unfelt, unconfessed sin is the true leprosy; but when sin is seen and felt, it has received its deathblow, and the Lord looks with eyes of mercy on the soul afflicted with it. Nothing is more deadly than self-righteousness, and nothing more hopeful than a broken heart. We must confess that we are “nothing else but sin,” for no confession short of this will be the whole truth. And if the Holy Spirit is at work in us, convincing us of sin, we won’t find it hard to admit this; it will spring from our lips of its own accord.

What comfort the text gives those under a deep sense of sin! Sin mourned and confessed, however black and foul, will never shut anyone out from the Lord Jesus. He will never turn away anyone who comes to him. Though dishonest as the thief, though unchaste as the woman who was a sinner, though fierce as Saul of Tarsus, though cruel as Manasseh, though rebellious as the prodigal, the great heart of love will look on the one who feels he has no soundness in him, and will pronounce him clean, when he trusts in Jesus crucified. Come to him, then, poor heavy-laden sinner,

modern:
Does Christ receive us when we come to him, in spite of all our past sinfulness? Does he never scold us for having tried every other refuge first? And is there no one on earth like him? Is he the best of all the good, the fairest of all the fair? Oh, then let’s praise him! Daughters of Jerusalem, praise him with tambourine and harp! Down with your idols; up with the Lord Jesus. Now let the banners of pomp and pride be trampled underfoot, but let the cross of Jesus, which the world frowns and sneers at, be lifted high. Oh, for a throne of ivory for our King Solomon! Let him be set on high forever, and let my soul sit at his footstool and kiss his feet and wash them with my tears.

Oh, how precious Christ is! How can it be that I have thought so little of him? How can I go elsewhere for joy or comfort when he is so full, so rich, so satisfying? Fellow believer, make a covenant with your heart that you will never leave him, and ask your Lord to seal it. Ask him to set you like a signet ring on his finger, and like a bracelet on his arm. Ask him to bind you to himself, the way a bride adorns herself with ornaments and a bridegroom puts on his jewels. I would live in Christ’s heart; in the clefts of that rock my soul would stay forever. The sparrow has found a house, and the swallow a nest for herself where she may lay her young, even your altars, O Lord of hosts, my King and my God; and so I too would make my nest, my home, in you. May the soul of your turtledove never go out from you again, but may I nestle close to you, O Jesus, my true and only rest.

modern:
Whether we praise God or not isn’t left up to us. Praise is what God most rightly deserves, and every Christian, having received his grace, is bound to praise God day by day. It’s true that we have no official rule for daily praise; we have no commandment laying down certain hours for song and thanksgiving. But the law written on the heart teaches us that it is right to praise God, and that unwritten command comes to us with as much force as if it had been carved on the tablets of stone, or handed to us from the top of thundering Sinai. Yes, it is the Christian’s *duty* to praise God. It isn’t only an enjoyable exercise; it is the absolute obligation of his life.

You who are always mourning, don’t think you are blameless in this, or imagine you can do your duty to your God without songs of praise. You are bound by the bonds of his love to bless his name as long as you live, and his praise should always be in your mouth; for you are blessed so that you may bless him. “This people have I formed for myself, they shall show forth my praise”; and if you don’t praise God, you aren’t bearing the fruit which he, as the divine Gardener, has a right to expect from you. So don’t leave your harp hanging on the willows; take it down and try, with a grateful heart, to bring out its loudest music. Get up and sing his praise. With every morning’s dawn lift up your notes of thanksgiving, and let every sunset be followed by your song. Wrap the earth in your praises; surround it with an atmosphere of melody, and God himself will listen from heaven and accept your music.

modern: Life is a precious thing, and even in its humblest form it is better than death. This truth is especially certain in spiritual things. It is better to be the least in the kingdom of heaven than the greatest outside it. The lowest degree of grace is better than the noblest growth of unregenerate nature. Where the Holy Spirit plants divine life in the soul, there is a precious deposit that none of the refinements of education can equal. The thief on the cross outranks Caesar on his throne; Lazarus among the dogs is better than Cicero among the senators; and the most uneducated Christian is, in the sight of God, superior to Plato. Life is the badge of nobility in the realm of spiritual things, and people without it are only coarser or finer specimens of the same lifeless material. They need to be made alive, for they are dead in trespasses and sins.

A living, loving gospel sermon, however unlearned its content and awkward its style, is better than the finest speech that lacks unction and power. A living dog keeps better watch than a dead lion and is more use to his master; and in the same way the poorest spiritual preacher is infinitely better than the polished orator who has no wisdom but the wisdom of words, no energy but the energy of sound. The same is true of our prayers and other acts of worship. If the Holy Spirit makes us alive in them, they are acceptable to God through Jesus Christ, even though we may think them worthless; while our grand performances, in which our hearts weren’t present, are like a dead lion: to the living God, they’re nothing but a rotting carcass. Oh, for living groans, living sighs, living despondencies, rather than lifeless songs and dead calms! Better anything than death. The snarling of the dog of hell will at least keep us awake; but dead faith and a dead profession, what greater curses can a person have? Make us alive, make us alive, O Lord!
